stem: A body executes simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is
options: proportional to displacement, directed away from the mean position
constant in size and directed towards the mean position
proportional to the square of displacement, towards the mean position
proportional to displacement, directed towards the mean position
explanation: SHM is defined by a = −ω²x: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from the mean position and always points back towards it (the minus sign). An acceleration directed away from the mean position would push the body further out, so it would not oscillate.

stem: A vibrating body completes one oscillation in 0.2 s. Its frequency is
explanation: Frequency is the number of oscillations per second, f = 1/T = 1/0.2 = 5 Hz. Writing 0.2 Hz confuses the period with the frequency.

stem: When a body in simple harmonic motion passes through its mean position, its
options: speed is maximum and acceleration is zero
speed is zero and acceleration is maximum
speed and acceleration are both maximum
speed and acceleration are both zero
explanation: At x = 0, a = −ω²x = 0, while v = ω√(A² − x²) takes its largest value ωA. Zero speed with maximum acceleration describes the extreme positions instead.

stem: At an extreme position of a body in simple harmonic motion, the
options: restoring force on the body is zero
explanation: At x = ±A the body is momentarily at rest, so KE = 0 and all the energy is potential, ½kA², its largest value. The restoring force −kx is also at its maximum there, not zero.

stem: A 0.4 kg mass attached to a spring of spring constant 40 N/m oscillates on a smooth horizontal surface. Its time period is
explanation: T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(0.4/40) = 2π√0.01 = 2π × 0.1 = 0.2π s (about 0.63 s). Inverting the ratio to √(k/m) = 10 gives 20π s.

stem: Taking g = 10 m/s², the time period of a simple pendulum of length 2.5 m is
explanation: T = 2π√(l/g) = 2π√(2.5/10) = 2π√0.25 = 2π × 0.5 = π s. Forgetting the square root gives 2π × 0.25 = π/2 s.

stem: Taking g = π² m/s², the length of a seconds pendulum (time period 2 s) is
explanation: From T = 2π√(l/g), l = gT²/4π² = π² × 4/4π² = 1 m. Using T = 1 s (the time for one swing, not a full oscillation) gives 0.25 m.

stem: If the length of a simple pendulum is made four times as great, its time period becomes
explanation: T = 2π√(l/g) is proportional to √l, so multiplying l by 4 multiplies T by √4 = 2. Four times as large would be true only if T were proportional to l.

stem: Fatima replaces the bob of a simple pendulum by one of twice the mass, keeping the length and the small amplitude the same. The time period becomes
explanation: T = 2π√(l/g) contains no mass: a heavier bob needs more force to accelerate, but its weight (the restoring force) increases in the same ratio. The √2 factor would apply to a mass-spring system, where T = 2π√(m/k).

stem: The mass attached to a spring is increased to four times its original value. The frequency of oscillation becomes
explanation: f = (1/2π)√(k/m), so f is proportional to 1/√m; with 4m, f becomes 1/√4 = ½ of the original. One quarter forgets the square root, and twice as large applies to the period, not the frequency.

stem: A particle executes SHM with amplitude 0.05 m and angular frequency 20 rad/s. Its maximum speed is
explanation: v(max) = ωA = 20 × 0.05 = 1 m/s, reached at the mean position. The value 20 is ω²A, the maximum acceleration in m/s², not the speed.

stem: A body oscillates in SHM with amplitude 8 cm and angular frequency 5 rad/s. Its maximum acceleration is
explanation: a(max) = ω²A = 25 × 0.08 = 2 m/s², at the extreme positions. The value 0.4 is ωA, the maximum speed in m/s, and 62.5 divides ω² by A instead of multiplying.

stem: A particle in SHM has amplitude 10 cm and angular frequency 4 rad/s. Its speed when its displacement is 6 cm is
explanation: v = ω√(A² − x²) = 4√(100 − 36) = 4 × 8 = 32 cm/s. The value 40 cm/s is the maximum speed ωA at the mean position, and 24 cm/s is ωx, which wrongly makes the speed grow with displacement.

stem: A particle executes SHM of amplitude A. Its speed is half of its maximum speed when its displacement from the mean position is
explanation: Set ω√(A² − x²) = ωA/2: A² − x² = A²/4, so x² = 3A²/4 and x = (√3/2)A. The tempting A/2 assumes speed falls linearly with displacement, which it does not.

stem: A particle executes SHM of amplitude A. Its kinetic energy equals its potential energy when its displacement is
explanation: PE = ½kx² and total E = ½kA². KE = PE means PE = E/2, so x² = A²/2 and x = A/√2. At x = A/2 the PE is only a quarter of the total energy.

stem: If the amplitude of a simple harmonic oscillator is doubled, keeping the spring and mass the same, its total energy becomes
explanation: Total energy E = ½kA² = ½mω²A² is proportional to A², so doubling A multiplies E by 4. The period does not change with amplitude, which is why one might wrongly think the energy is unchanged.

stem: A 0.5 kg block attached to a spring of spring constant 200 N/m oscillates with amplitude 10 cm on a smooth surface. Its kinetic energy when the displacement is 5 cm is
explanation: Total energy = ½kA² = ½ × 200 × 0.1² = 1 J, and PE at x = 0.05 m = ½ × 200 × 0.05² = 0.25 J, so KE = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75 J. The value 0.25 J is the PE at that point, and 0.5 J wrongly assumes energy shares in proportion to x rather than x².

stem: In simple harmonic motion, the phase difference between the displacement and the velocity is
explanation: With x = A sin ωt, v = ωA cos ωt = ωA sin(ωt + π/2), so velocity leads displacement by π/2. That is why v is maximum when x = 0 and zero when x is maximum.

stem: In simple harmonic motion, the phase difference between the displacement and the acceleration is
explanation: a = −ω²x, so acceleration is always opposite to displacement: a = ω²A sin(ωt + π). The phase difference is π. A difference of π/2 is between displacement and velocity, not acceleration.

stem: The displacement of a particle is given by x = 0.04 sin(10πt) metre, with t in seconds. The frequency of the motion is
explanation: Compare with x = A sin ωt: ω = 10π rad/s, so f = ω/2π = 10π/2π = 5 Hz. Reading 10π directly as the frequency mistakes angular frequency for frequency, and 0.2 is the period in seconds.

stem: A particle moves according to x = 3 sin(2t + π/4) cm, with t in seconds. Its maximum acceleration is
explanation: Here A = 3 cm and ω = 2 rad/s, so a(max) = ω²A = 4 × 3 = 12 cm/s². The initial phase π/4 does not affect the maximum value. The value 6 is ωA, the maximum speed in cm/s.

stem: A particle moves round a circle of radius 5 cm at a steady 2 revolutions per second. The projection of the particle on a diameter executes SHM. The maximum speed of this projection is
explanation: The projection has amplitude equal to the radius, 5 cm, and ω = 2πf = 4π rad/s, so v(max) = ωA = 4π × 5 = 20π cm/s. This equals the particle's own speed on the circle. Using ω = 2π (1 rev/s) gives 10π cm/s.

stem: A spring stretches by 10 cm when a mass is hung from it at rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², the time period with which the mass oscillates up and down on this spring is
explanation: At equilibrium kx = mg, so m/k = x/g = 0.1/10 = 0.01 s², and T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π × 0.1 = 0.2π s. The mass itself is not needed. The option 0.1π s drops the 2 of 2π, and 2π s comes from putting the extension in centimetres, √(10/10) = 1.

stem: A mass on a single spring oscillates with period T₀. The same mass is now hung from two such identical springs joined end to end (in series). The new period is
explanation: Two identical springs in series have effective constant k/2 (each stretches by the same force, so the extension doubles). T = 2π√(m/(k/2)) = √2 × 2π√(m/k) = √2 T₀. T₀/√2 is the result for the parallel arrangement, where the effective constant is 2k.

stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with period T₀. The spring is cut into two equal halves and the same mass is attached to one half. The new period is
explanation: Half the spring stretches half as much for the same force, so its spring constant is 2k. T = 2π√(m/2k) = T₀/√2. The answer T₀/2 forgets the square root in the period formula.

stem: Free oscillations of a body are oscillations
options: at its natural frequency with no external periodic force
at the frequency of an applied periodic force
that grow in amplitude without any limit
that occur only when the body is in a vacuum
explanation: A body displaced and then left alone oscillates freely at its own natural frequency, which depends only on its properties (for example m and k, or l and g). Oscillations at the frequency of an applied periodic force are forced oscillations.

stem: When a body is made to oscillate by an external periodic force, it vibrates with
options: its own natural frequency in every case
the frequency of the driving force
a frequency that keeps on rising
explanation: In forced oscillations the driver imposes its own frequency on the body after the initial motion dies away. The natural frequency matters only in deciding how large the amplitude is; when the two are equal, resonance occurs.

stem: Resonance occurs when
options: the driving frequency equals the natural frequency
the driving force is removed completely
the damping force becomes very large
the amplitude of the driver is zero
explanation: At resonance the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, so energy is fed in at exactly the right moment in each cycle and the amplitude becomes maximum. Large damping reduces the resonant amplitude rather than causing resonance.

stem: Damping in an oscillating system
options: gradually reduces the amplitude as energy is lost
explanation: Damping forces such as friction and air resistance do negative work, converting the oscillator's mechanical energy into heat. Since E is proportional to A², the amplitude steadily decreases. A constant amplitude would need no losses, or an energy supply as in forced oscillations.

stem: Tuning a radio receiver to pick up one particular station is an example of
explanation: Turning the tuning knob changes the natural frequency of the receiver's electrical circuit. When it equals the frequency of the station's waves, that signal produces a large response while other stations produce very little, which is resonance.

stem: For a driven oscillator, increasing the damping makes the graph of amplitude against driving frequency
explanation: With more damping, more energy is lost per cycle, so the maximum amplitude at resonance is smaller and the response is spread over a wider range of frequencies. Light damping gives the high, sharp peak.

stem: Soldiers marching across a bridge are told to break step. The main reason is to avoid
explanation: Marching in step applies a periodic force to the bridge. If its frequency matched the bridge's natural frequency, resonance would build up a dangerously large amplitude. Breaking step makes the forces irregular, so no single frequency is driven.

stem: Shock absorbers in a car's suspension are a practical use of
options: forced oscillation at the natural frequency
explanation: Shock absorbers convert the energy of the springs' oscillations into heat in oil, so the car body stops bouncing quickly after a bump. Resonance or driving at the natural frequency would make the bouncing worse, not better.

stem: A displaced oscillating system that returns to its equilibrium position in the shortest possible time, without oscillating, is said to be
explanation: Critical damping is just enough to prevent any overshoot, so the system returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating; car suspensions are designed close to it. Light damping still allows several oscillations of falling amplitude, and an undamped system oscillates forever.

stem: A simple pendulum has a period T on the Earth. On the Moon, where the acceleration due to gravity is one sixth of that on the Earth, the period of the same pendulum is
explanation: T = 2π√(l/g) is proportional to 1/√g, so with g/6 the period becomes √6 times larger, about 2.45T. The pendulum swings more slowly where gravity is weaker; T/√6 would mean it swings faster.

stem: A simple pendulum has period T in a stationary lift. Taking g = 10 m/s², its period when the lift accelerates upwards at 5 m/s² is
explanation: In a lift accelerating upwards the effective gravity is g + a = 15 m/s². Since T is proportional to 1/√g, T′ = T√(10/15) = T√(2/3), shorter than T. Using g − a = 5 m/s² would give T√2, the result for downward acceleration.

stem: A simple pendulum with period T on the ground is taken into a lift that is falling freely. In the lift, the pendulum
explanation: In free fall the effective gravity is g − g = 0, so there is no restoring force and T = 2π√(l/0) becomes infinite: displaced, the bob simply stays where it is. A period of zero would mean infinitely fast swings, the opposite of what happens.

stem: Two simple pendulums at the same place have lengths 1 m and 4 m. The ratio of their frequencies (shorter : longer) is
explanation: f = (1/2π)√(g/l), so f is proportional to 1/√l: f₁/f₂ = √(4/1) = 2. The shorter pendulum swings faster. The ratio 1 : 2 is for the periods, not the frequencies.

stem: A mass on a spring of spring constant 50 N/m is displaced 4 cm from its equilibrium position. The restoring force on it is
options: 2 N away from the mean position
explanation: By Hooke's law F = −kx = −50 × 0.04 = −2 N: magnitude 2 N, directed opposite to the displacement, that is towards the mean position. Using x = 4 (in cm) gives 200 N, and the force can never point away from the mean position in SHM.

stem: A particle executes SHM with angular frequency 10 rad/s. The magnitude of its acceleration when its displacement is 3 cm is
explanation: a = ω²x = 100 × 0.03 = 3 m/s² (directed towards the mean position). Using ωx instead of ω²x gives 0.3 m/s², and leaving x in centimetres gives 300.

stem: A body in SHM has an acceleration of 16 m/s² when its displacement is 4 cm. Its time period is
explanation: ω² = a/x = 16/0.04 = 400, so ω = 20 rad/s and T = 2π/ω = 2π/20 = π/10 s. Taking T = π/ω forgets the factor 2 and gives π/20 s.

stem: A particle in SHM has a maximum speed of 2 m/s and a maximum acceleration of 8 m/s². Its amplitude is
explanation: a(max)/v(max) = ω²A/ωA = ω = 8/2 = 4 rad/s, and then A = v(max)/ω = 2/4 = 0.5 m. The value 4 is ω, not the amplitude, and 0.25 m divides by ω twice.

stem: A particle in SHM of period T starts from the mean position. The shortest time it takes to reach a displacement of half the amplitude is
explanation: x = A sin ωt = A/2 gives ωt = π/6, so t = (π/6)/(2π/T) = T/12. It is not T/8 (half of the quarter period T/4), because the particle moves fastest near the mean position and covers the first half-amplitude quickly.

stem: A particle in SHM of period T starts from an extreme position. The shortest time it takes to reach a displacement of half the amplitude is
explanation: From the extreme, x = A cos ωt = A/2 gives ωt = π/3, so t = (π/3)/(2π/T) = T/6. The particle is slow near the extreme, so it takes longer than the T/12 needed for the half-amplitude next to the mean position.

stem: A particle in SHM of amplitude A and angular frequency ω is at its positive extreme position at t = 0. Its displacement at time t is
explanation: At t = 0, A cos 0 = A, the positive extreme, as required. A sin ωt and A sin(ωt + π) both give x = 0 at t = 0 (start at the mean position), and −A cos ωt starts at the negative extreme.

stem: The phase of a particle executing SHM tells us
options: its displacement and direction of motion at that instant
explanation: The phase, the angle ωt + φ in x = A sin(ωt + φ), fixes where the particle is in its cycle: its displacement and which way it is moving. The energy depends on amplitude, not on phase.

stem: For a mass-spring system in SHM, a graph of potential energy against displacement is
options: a parabola with its minimum at the mean position
a straight line through the origin
a parabola with its maximum at the mean position
explanation: U = ½kx² is a parabola, zero at x = 0 and rising to ½kA² at the extremes. A horizontal line describes the total energy, and the kinetic energy curve is the inverted parabola with its maximum at the mean position.

stem: A body oscillates in SHM with frequency f. Its kinetic energy varies periodically with frequency
explanation: K = ½mv² with v = ωA cos ωt gives K = ½mω²A² cos²ωt = ¼mω²A²(1 + cos 2ωt), which repeats at 2ω, that is frequency 2f. Physically, KE is maximum twice per oscillation, once each way through the mean position.

stem: In an undamped simple harmonic oscillator, the total mechanical energy
options: is maximum at the mean position only
is zero at the extreme positions
varies as the square of the displacement
explanation: Without damping, energy only changes form: KE + PE = ½kA² at every point. It is the PE, not the total, that varies as x², and the KE, not the total, that is zero at the extremes.

stem: The motion of a simple pendulum is simple harmonic only for small amplitudes because
options: the tension in the string vanishes at small angles
air resistance disappears for small swings
the mass of the bob changes at large angles
sin θ ≈ θ (in radians) only when θ is small
explanation: The restoring force is mg sin θ. Only for small θ is sin θ ≈ θ = x/l, giving F = −(mg/l)x, which is proportional to displacement as SHM requires. At large angles sin θ is noticeably less than θ, so the motion is periodic but not simple harmonic.

stem: The time period of a mass-spring system does not depend on
options: the mass attached to the spring
explanation: T = 2π√(m/k) contains only the mass and the spring constant, so a larger or smaller amplitude gives the same period (as long as Hooke's law holds). A bigger amplitude simply means a larger maximum speed.

stem: A body vibrates with a frequency of 50 Hz. Its angular frequency is
explanation: ω = 2πf = 2π × 50 = 100π rad/s. Writing ω = πf gives 50π, and 25/π comes from dividing by 2π instead of multiplying.

stem: The amplitude of a simple harmonic motion is
options: the maximum displacement from the mean position
the total distance covered in one full oscillation
the distance between the two extreme positions
the time taken for one oscillation
explanation: Amplitude A is the greatest distance of the body from its mean position, reached at each extreme. The distance between the two extremes is 2A, and the distance covered in one full oscillation is 4A.

stem: A particle executes SHM with amplitude 5 cm. The total distance it travels in one complete oscillation is
explanation: In one oscillation the particle goes from the mean position to one extreme, back, to the other extreme and back: 4A = 4 × 5 = 20 cm. Zero is its displacement after a full cycle, not the distance travelled.

stem: Which of the following motions is simple harmonic (for small displacements)?
options: A mass vibrating on a light spring
A ball bouncing on a hard floor
The Earth moving round the Sun
A car moving at constant speed on a road
explanation: A mass on a spring feels F = −kx, a restoring force proportional to displacement, which is the condition for SHM. A bouncing ball has a constant downward acceleration between bounces, and the Earth's orbit is periodic but its acceleration is not proportional to a displacement from a mean position.

stem: The displacement-time graph of a particle executing SHM is
explanation: The displacement is x = A sin(ωt + φ), so the graph is a sine (sinusoidal) curve repeating every period T. A parabola is the PE-displacement graph, not the displacement-time graph.

stem: The length of a simple pendulum is increased by 21 %. Its time period increases by
explanation: T is proportional to √l, so the new period is √1.21 = 1.1 times the old one, an increase of 10 %. Forgetting the square root gives 21 %, and squaring instead (1.21² ≈ 1.46) gives 46 %.

stem: A 2 kg body executes SHM with angular frequency 5 rad/s and amplitude 0.2 m. Its total energy is
explanation: E = ½mω²A² = ½ × 2 × 25 × 0.04 = 1 J. Dropping the ½ gives 2 J, and forgetting to square the amplitude gives ½ × 2 × 25 × 0.2 = 5 J.

stem: When an extra 0.3 kg is added to the mass hanging on a spring, the period of vertical oscillation doubles. The original mass was
explanation: T is proportional to √m, so doubling T needs four times the mass: m + 0.3 = 4m, giving m = 0.1 kg. Assuming T proportional to m gives m + 0.3 = 2m and m = 0.3 kg.

stem: A pendulum clock keeps correct time in winter. In summer its pendulum is 0.2 % longer. There are 86 400 s in a day. In summer the clock
explanation: T is proportional to √l, so a 0.2 % longer pendulum has a period about 0.1 % longer (√1.002 ≈ 1.001). The clock ticks slower and loses 0.001 × 86 400 ≈ 86 s per day. Forgetting the square root gives 173 s, and a longer period can never make the clock gain.

stem: For small swings, the time period of a simple pendulum depends on
options: the length of the string and g
explanation: T = 2π√(l/g): only the length and the acceleration due to gravity appear. Mass and material cancel out, and for small angles the period is independent of amplitude.

stem: A pendulum makes 30 complete oscillations in 15 s. Its time period is
explanation: T = total time/number of oscillations = 15/30 = 0.5 s. The value 2 is the frequency in hertz (30/15), not the period.

stem: For a mass oscillating on a horizontal spring, at the equilibrium position
explanation: At x = 0 the spring is at its natural length, so elastic PE, restoring force and acceleration are all zero, and all the energy is kinetic. The PE, force and acceleration are greatest at the extreme positions.

stem: A singer holds a note that shatters a thin wine glass. This happens because of
explanation: When the frequency of the note equals the natural frequency of the glass, the sound drives the glass at resonance and its vibration amplitude builds up until the glass breaks. Damping would reduce the vibration, not increase it.

stem: For a mass m on a spring of spring constant k, the angular frequency of oscillation is
explanation: From ma = −kx, a = −(k/m)x, and comparing with a = −ω²x gives ω = √(k/m). The expression 2π√(m/k) is the time period, not the angular frequency.

stem: A 1 kg mass oscillates on a spring of spring constant 100 N/m. Its frequency of oscillation is
explanation: ω = √(k/m) = √100 = 10 rad/s, so f = ω/2π = 10/2π = 5/π Hz (about 1.6 Hz). The value π/5 is the period in seconds, and 10 is ω, not f.

stem: On the Earth (taking g = π² m/s²) a seconds pendulum is 1 m long. On a planet where the acceleration due to gravity is one quarter of the Earth's value, the length of a seconds pendulum is
explanation: For the same period T = 2π√(l/g), l/g must stay the same, so l is proportional to g: 1 × ¼ = 0.25 m. Taking l proportional to √g gives 0.5 m, and 4 m inverts the relation.

stem: A 1 kg mass on a spring of spring constant 400 N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Its maximum speed is
explanation: ω = √(k/m) = √400 = 20 rad/s, so v(max) = ωA = 20 × 0.1 = 2 m/s. Using ω² = 400 instead of ω gives 40, which is the maximum acceleration in m/s².

stem: A spring of spring constant 100 N/m carries a mass that oscillates with amplitude 0.2 m. The total energy of the oscillation is
explanation: E = ½kA² = ½ × 100 × 0.04 = 2 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 4 J, and forgetting to square A gives ½ × 100 × 0.2 = 10 J.

stem: The displacement of a particle is x = 5 sin(4πt + π/3) cm, with t in seconds. Its phase at t = 1/12 s is
explanation: Phase = 4πt + π/3 = 4π/12 + π/3 = π/3 + π/3 = 2π/3. The value π/3 is only the initial phase (at t = 0).

stem: A pendulum left swinging in air gradually comes to rest. Its mechanical energy has mainly been
options: destroyed by the pull of gravity
stored as extra PE of the bob
given to the Earth as kinetic energy
changed into heat by air resistance and friction
explanation: Air resistance and friction at the support damp the motion: they do negative work and turn the oscillation energy into internal energy (heat) of the air and the support. Energy is not destroyed, and the bob ends at its lowest point, so it has less PE, not more.

stem: Bilal wants a child's swing to go higher using only small pushes. The pushes should be given
options: once every natural period of the swing
whenever the swing moves towards him
explanation: Pushing once each cycle, always in the direction of motion, drives the swing at its natural frequency, so energy is added every cycle and the amplitude grows (resonance). Pushing when the swing moves towards him opposes the motion and takes energy out.

stem: A particle executes SHM of amplitude A. When its displacement is A/2, the ratio of its kinetic energy to its potential energy is
explanation: PE = ½k(A/2)² = ¼ of the total ½kA², so KE = ¾ of the total and KE : PE = 3 : 1. Reversing the ratio to 1 : 3 gives the situation at x = (√3/2)A.

stem: A particle in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and maximum speed 10 cm/s. Its speed when the displacement is 3 cm is
explanation: ω = v(max)/A = 10/5 = 2 rad/s, so v = ω√(A² − x²) = 2√(25 − 9) = 2 × 4 = 8 cm/s. Using ω(A − x) = 2 × 2 gives 4 cm/s, and 6 cm/s is ωx, which makes the speed grow with displacement.

stem: A mass hung on a spring produces a static extension of 25 cm. A simple pendulum has the same time period as the mass oscillating on this spring. The length of the pendulum is
explanation: At equilibrium kx = mg, so m/k = x/g and T = 2π√(x/g). A pendulum has T = 2π√(l/g), so equal periods need l = x = 25 cm. Doubling to 50 cm or quadrupling to 100 cm would wrongly bring in factors from the spring energy formula.
